gorakh.name: Dr. Gorakh Mandrupkar
gorakh.title: Reproductive medicine and infertility specialist
gorakh.essence: The doctor who explains until it finally makes sense.
gorakh.intro: Dr. Gorakh believes that understanding your treatment is part of feeling safe in it. He takes time to explain the science plainly, answer every question, and build a plan around the couple in front of him.
gorakh.biography:
Dr. Gorakh Gopalkrishna Mandrupkar is a distinguished Reproductive Medicine and Infertility Specialist with over 20 years of experience in infertility management. He was awarded the Gold Medal in Gynecology by Pune University in 2004 and has been serving as a Consultant in Reproductive Medicine since March 2006.



Over the course of his career, Dr. Mandrupkar has helped more than 2,000 couples achieve successful pregnancies through advanced fertility treatments and personalized patient care.



Academic & Training Excellence

• Gold Medallist in Gynecology, Pune University (2004)

• Consultant in Reproductive Medicine since March 2006

• Over 20 years of experience in infertility management

• Successfully treated more than 2,000 infertile couples

• Director of a FOGSI-recognized IVF Training Centre for the past 10 years, where numerous gynecologists have received specialized training in IUI and IVF techniques.



Research & Innovation

Dr. Mandrupkar has made a significant contribution to maternal healthcare by developing the HDP Gestosis Score, a simple and innovative screening tool for identifying women at risk of preeclampsia (pregnancy-induced hypertension). Preeclampsia is a major cause of maternal mortality worldwide, accounting for nearly 19% of maternal deaths, according to WHO reports. The HDP Gestosis Score has been adopted by the National Health Mission (NHM), Government of India, for clinical use.



Know more about the Gestosis Score



Professional Leadership

Dr. Mandrupkar serves as an honorary member on various national committees of the Government of India and leading national organizations of gynecologists, contributing to the advancement of women's healthcare and reproductive medicine.



Commitment to Women's Health

In addition to providing comprehensive fertility care, Mandrupkar Clinic actively conducts clinical research aimed at improving women's health and advancing evidence-based reproductive medicine. The clinic remains committed to delivering ethical, innovative, and patient-centered care.

saie.intro: Dr. Saie brings steadiness to the moments that feel most uncertain. Her work in high-risk obstetrics and reproductive medicine is grounded in careful attention, calm communication, and the conviction that every patient deserves to feel heard.
saie.biography:
Dr. Saie Gorakh Mandrupkar completed her postgraduate degree in Obstetrics and Gynecology from Pune University in 2005. With over 20 years of clinical experience, she specializes in high-risk obstetrics, infertility management, and reproductive medicine.



She has successfully helped more than 2,000 couples achieve their dream of parenthood through comprehensive infertility evaluation and advanced fertility treatments.



Dr. Saie Mandrupkar has extensive expertise in managing high-risk pregnancies, including:

• IVF pregnancies

• Pregnancy complicated by diabetes

• Pregnancy with hypertension

• Recurrent pregnancy loss

• Other complex maternal and fetal conditions



She is committed to providing evidence-based, compassionate, and personalized care throughout every stage of a woman's reproductive journey—from fertility treatment to safe motherhood.



In addition to her clinical practice, Dr. Saie Mandrupkar actively participates in clinical research at Mandrupkar Clinic, contributing to advancements in women's healthcare and ensuring that patients benefit from the latest medical knowledge and treatment approaches.

UnderstandingIVF.heading: What happens, step by step — and why.
UnderstandingIVF.body: IVF can feel overwhelming from the outside. Here are the six steps as they actually unfold, in plain language.

stimulation.heading: Preparing your body
stimulation.body: A gentle head start. Light medication helps your ovaries prepare more eggs than usual, with care at every check-in.

retrieval.heading: Collecting the eggs
retrieval.body: A short, calm procedure under anesthesia. The matured eggs are gently collected — most people feel only mild discomfort.

fertilisation.heading: Egg meets sperm
fertilisation.body: In the lab, egg and sperm are brought together — the quiet beginning of a possible embryo.

culture.heading: The embryo grows
culture.body: Over a few days, embryos develop under close watch, and the healthiest is chosen with care.

transfer.heading: The transfer
transfer.body: A quick, painless step. The embryo is gently placed in the womb — no anesthesia, no bed rest needed.

wait.heading: The wait, together
wait.body: About two weeks until the test. The hardest wait — and the one we walk through with you.

UnderstandingIVF.closeBody: By the time treatment begins, you’ll understand every step — and that clarity changes everything.

MythsFacts.heading: The questions almost everyone asks.
MythsFacts.body: If something here has been on your mind, you’re not alone — these are the things couples ask us most. Honest answers, in plain language.

q1.q: Are IVF babies as healthy as other babies?
q1.a: Yes. Millions of healthy children have been born through IVF worldwide. An IVF baby is just as healthy — and just as loved — as any other.

q2.a: Not anymore. We usually transfer a single healthy embryo, so most IVF pregnancies are a single baby.

q3.a: Most people feel only mild discomfort. The egg-collection step is done under anesthesia, so you won’t feel pain during it.

q4.q: Is IVF only about the woman?
q4.a: No. Fertility challenges are just as often related to the man — or both partners. We look at the whole picture, together, without blame.

q5.a: It’s one of the most important factors — which is exactly why understanding your options early gives you the most choices. But every story is different, and 40 is not a closed door.

q6.q: Do I need complete bed rest after the embryo transfer?
q6.a: No. Normal daily life is safe. We may simply ask you to avoid heavy lifting or intense exercise for a short while.

q7.a: With a conversation — no commitment. We listen to your story, answer your questions, and only then talk about what (if anything) comes next.

MythsFacts.closeBody: Still wondering about something? The best answers are the ones about your situation.

pcos.metaTitle: PCOS — signs, causes, and how we treat it
pcos.metaDescription: PCOS is a common, treatable hormonal condition that can affect your periods and fertility. The signs to watch for, why it happens, and how we treat it — with a healthy lifestyle at the heart.
pcos.title: PCOS
pcos.excerpt: A common, treatable hormonal condition that can affect your periods and fertility. The signs to watch for, why it happens, and how we treat it.
pcos.intro: PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome) — now also called PMOS (Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome). PCOS is a common condition that affects a woman's hormones. It can make periods irregular and may make it harder to become pregnant. It can also cause weight gain, acne, and extra hair growth on the face or body. PCOS can be treated, and most women with PCOS can live a healthy life.

signs.heading: Common signs and symptoms
items: Irregular or missed periods
Difficulty getting pregnant
Weight gain or difficulty losing weight
Pimples (acne)
Extra hair on the face, chest, or tummy
Hair thinning on the scalp
Dark skin around the neck or underarms
signs.note: Not every woman with PCOS has all these symptoms.

why.heading: Why does PCOS happen?
why.body: The exact cause is not known. It may run in families. Many women with PCOS have a problem called insulin resistance, where the body does not use insulin properly. This can lead to weight gain and make PCOS symptoms worse.

diagnosis.heading: How is PCOS diagnosed?
items: Ask about your periods and symptoms
Examine you
Recommend blood tests
Suggest an ultrasound scan if needed

treatment.heading: How is PCOS treated?

lifestyle.heading: Healthy lifestyle
lifestyle.intro: A healthy lifestyle is the most important treatment.
items: Eat healthy home-cooked meals
Eat more vegetables, fruits, whole grains, pulses, and lean protein
Reduce sweets, sugary drinks, and junk food
Exercise for at least 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week
Losing even a small amount of weight can improve periods and increase the chance of pregnancy

treatment.mantra: My mantra: Eat less, walk more!

medicines.heading: Medicines
items: Make your periods regular
Help with acne or unwanted hair growth
Improve insulin resistance
Help you become pregnant if you are planning a baby
medicines.note: Always take medicines only as advised by us or the concerned doctor.

regular.heading: Why is regular treatment important?
regular.intro: If PCOS is not treated, it may increase the risk of:
items: Diabetes (high blood sugar)
High blood pressure
High cholesterol
Problems with pregnancy
Cancer of the uterus (womb) if periods are absent for a long time
regular.closing: Regular check-ups help prevent these problems.

visit.heading: When should you visit us?
items: Do not get your period for more than 3 months (and are not pregnant)
Have very heavy or prolonged bleeding
Are trying to become pregnant without success
Notice rapid weight gain, severe acne, or increased facial hair

remember.heading: Remember
items: PCOS is common and treatable
Healthy eating, regular exercise, and taking medicines as prescribed can control PCOS
Regular follow-up with your doctor is important to keep you healthy
It will reduce future health problems like diabetes, high blood pressure, and some gynecological cancers

male-fertility.metaTitle: Male infertility — causes, tests, and treatment
male-fertility.metaDescription: Male-factor infertility is common and often very treatable. The causes, the simple checks, what you can do to help, and when to see a doctor.
male-fertility.title: Male infertility
male-fertility.excerpt: Male-factor infertility is common and often very treatable. The causes, the simple checks, and what men can do to help.
male-fertility.intro: Male infertility means a man has trouble helping his partner become pregnant, even after trying for 1 year with regular unprotected sex.

about.heading: What is male factor infertility?
about.body: Male infertility means a man has trouble helping his partner become pregnant, even after trying for 1 year with regular unprotected sex.

causes.heading: What causes it?
items: Low sperm count
Weak or slow-moving sperm
Blockage in the sperm tubes
Infection
Hormone problems
Smoking, alcohol, drugs, or some medicines
Being overweight
Swollen veins around the testicles (varicocele)

signs.heading: What are the signs?
signs.body: Most men do not have any symptoms. The only sign may be difficulty having a baby.

checked.heading: How is it checked?
items: A physical examination
A semen test (to check sperm)
Blood tests for hormones and general health
An ultrasound if needed

treated.heading: Can it be treated?
treated.intro: Yes. Treatment depends on the cause and may include:
items: Medicines
Surgery (if needed)
Healthy lifestyle changes
Fertility treatments if required

doYou.heading: What can you do?
items: Stop smoking and avoid tobacco
Limit or avoid alcohol
Eat healthy food
Exercise regularly
Maintain a healthy weight
Get enough sleep
Avoid too much heat around the testicles

doctor.heading: When should you see a doctor?
items: If you have problems with erection or ejaculation
If you have been trying for 1 year and no pregnancy
If you have pain or swelling in the testicles

remember.heading: Remember
remember.line: Male infertility is common, and many men can be treated successfully.

recurrent-pregnancy-loss.metaTitle: Recurrent pregnancy loss — causes, tests, and hope
recurrent-pregnancy-loss.metaDescription: Recurrent miscarriage — two or more losses — is more common than many realise, and a healthy pregnancy is often still possible. The causes, tests, and treatment.
recurrent-pregnancy-loss.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss
recurrent-pregnancy-loss.excerpt: Recurrent miscarriage — two or more losses — is more common than many realise, and a healthy pregnancy is often still possible.
recurrent-pregnancy-loss.intro: Recurrent pregnancy loss means having two or more miscarriages. It is more common than many people realize, and in many cases, a healthy pregnancy is still possible.

why.heading: Why does it happen?
items: Problems with the baby's chromosomes (most common)
Problems with the shape of the uterus
Hormone problems (such as thyroid disease or diabetes)
Certain blood-clotting or immune conditions
Sometimes, no cause is found

tests.heading: What tests may be needed?
items: Blood tests for associated medical conditions
An ultrasound scan of the uterus
Tests for certain medical conditions
Special tests for APLAS, ANA, ENA or thrombophilia markers
Sometimes, genetic tests for the couple or the pregnancy tissue

treated.heading: Can it be treated?
treated.intro: Yes. Treatment depends on the cause and may include:
items: Medicines for thyroid disease, diabetes, or blood-clotting disorders
Surgery to correct some uterine problems
Close monitoring during the next pregnancy

chances.heading: What are the chances of a healthy baby?
chances.body: The good news is that most women with recurrent pregnancy loss go on to have a healthy baby, especially with proper medical care and follow-up.

doctor.heading: When should you see a doctor?
doctor.body: If you have had two or more miscarriages, consult an obstetrician or fertility specialist for evaluation and advice.

remember.heading: Remember
remember.line: Having recurrent miscarriages does not mean you cannot have a successful pregnancy. Early medical care and support can improve your chances.

what-ivf-really-is.metaTitle: Understanding IVF: a guide for your journey
what-ivf-really-is.metaDescription: A plain-language, step-by-step guide to IVF — all six phases, from preparing your body to the pregnancy test — written to explain exactly what to expect.
what-ivf-really-is.title: Understanding IVF: a guide for your journey
what-ivf-really-is.excerpt: A plain-language, step-by-step guide to IVF — all six phases, from preparing your body to the pregnancy test — so you know exactly what to expect.
what-ivf-really-is.intro:
Hello. If you are reading this, you are likely considering In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF) to help grow your family. It is completely normal to feel a mix of hope, excitement, and anxiety right now. This guide is written to explain the IVF process in plain, everyday language so you know exactly what to expect.

Think of IVF as a way to help nature along. 'In vitro' simply means 'outside the body' or in a laboratory. In short, we take eggs from the ovaries and mix them with sperm — or inject the sperm into the eggs (ICSI) — in our lab to create embryos. We then place the healthiest embryo back into your uterus when it is ready to receive it.

phase1.heading: Phase 1: Preparing your body
phase1.body: Before we begin the actual IVF cycle, we need to understand your unique reproductive health. This preparation stage ensures we customise the treatment plan specifically for you.
phase1.quote: Like plants, good preparation of the land before sowing the seeds gives the best yield — this phase is just as crucial.
items: Ovarian reserve testing: done by simple blood tests and a pelvic ultrasound on day 2 or 3 of your period.
Semen analysis: we test a semen sample to check the count, shape, and movement of the sperm. You can see them on screen.
Uterine exam: we examine the inside of your uterus using an ultrasound or a small 4 mm hysteroscope to ensure the inner lining is safe to welcome an embryo.
Lifestyle modifications: we will ask you to start prenatal vitamins, maintain a balanced diet, avoid alcohol, and stop smoking.

phase2.heading: Phase 2: Ovarian stimulation (growing the eggs)
phase2.body: In a natural monthly cycle, your body usually matures just one or two eggs. For IVF, we want to grow multiple eggs at once to increase your chances of success.
items: Hormone injections: you can take these yourself, under the skin of your belly or thigh, to encourage your ovaries to grow multiple egg follicles.
Regular monitoring: you will visit our clinic 2–3 times to monitor progress. With blood tests and ultrasounds, we watch the follicles grow and adjust your medication doses safely.
The trigger shot: once the follicles reach the ideal size, you take one final, precisely timed injection (the "trigger shot") that brings the eggs to full maturity, ready for collection.
phase2.note: There is no need for daily visits to the clinic.

phase3.heading: Phase 3: Egg retrieval (the collection)
phase3.body: The egg retrieval is a minor surgical procedure performed at our clinic. It takes about 20 minutes, and you will not feel any pain during the process, as it is done under a light anaesthetic or sedative so that you are completely asleep and comfortable.
items: Ultrasound guidance: a thin ultrasound probe is inserted into the vagina to clearly see your ovaries and the mature follicles.
Gentle suction: using a very fine, specialised needle attached to the probe, the fluid — and the egg inside it — is gently drawn out of each follicle.
Recovery: you will rest for an hour or two and be discharged the same day.

phase4.heading: Phase 4: Fertilisation and embryo development
phase4.body: While you are resting from your retrieval, our embryologist takes over the next steps. This is where the magic happens behind the scenes over the next 3 to 6 days.
items: IVF with conventional insemination: we place thousands of healthy sperm in a dish alongside the retrieved eggs and let them fertilise naturally.
ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection): if the sperm count is low or weak, our embryologist uses a tiny needle to inject a single, healthy sperm directly into each mature egg to help it fertilise.

The incubation phase: the fertilised eggs become embryos. We place them in advanced incubators that mimic the warmth and environment of a human body, monitoring their growth as they divide into multiple cells.

phase5.heading: Phase 5: The embryo transfer
phase5.body: The embryo transfer is the simplest and most exciting part of the medical process.
items: Selecting the best embryo: together, we choose 1 or 2 of the healthiest embryos to transfer. Remaining high-quality embryos can be frozen for your future use.
The procedure: under abdominal ultrasound guidance, the embryo(s) are transferred using a very soft, small catheter. You can watch this live on screen.

Immediate return to routine: the transfer takes less than 10 minutes. You can get up right away, walk around, and go home to rest. You do not need strict bed rest, but we recommend avoiding heavy lifting, intense workouts, and bumpy journeys.

phase6.heading: Phase 6: The 15-day wait
phase6.body: The final phase requires the most patience. Correct and timely use of progesterone medications, along with other supportive medicines, helps the embryo implant into the uterine lining naturally.
items: Managing anxiety: this waiting period can feel emotionally difficult. We encourage you to focus on light activities and stay connected with loved ones. Surrender to Supreme Nature and pamper yourself — this will help you fulfil your dream of parenthood.
The official pregnancy test: for a day-3 embryo transfer, the hormone HCG is measured in blood to confirm pregnancy 15 days after the transfer; for a day-5 transfer, 13 days after.

support.heading: Emotional support and next steps
support.body: IVF is a physical journey, but it is also an emotional rollercoaster. Our entire clinical team — including our dedicated nursing staff and counsellors — is here to support you through every single step, question, and milestone. If you are ready to begin, our next step is to schedule your initial consultation and baseline blood tests. Let's take this journey together, one step at a time.

ArticlePcos.metaDescription: PCOS is a common, treatable hormonal condition. Learn the signs, why it happens, how we diagnose and treat it, and when to see a doctor at IVF Master.
ArticlePcos.intro: PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome) — now also called PMOS (Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome). PCOS is a common condition that affects a woman's hormones. It can make periods irregular and may make it harder to become pregnant. It can also cause weight gain, acne, and extra hair growth on the face or body. PCOS can be treated, and most women with PCOS can live a healthy life.
signs: Weight gain or difficulty losing weight
Extra hair on the face, chest, or tummy
Dark skin around the neck or underarms
ArticlePcos.signsNote: Not every woman with PCOS has all these symptoms.
ArticlePcos.whyBody: The exact cause is not known. It may run in families. Many women with PCOS have a problem called insulin resistance, where the body does not use insulin properly. This can lead to weight gain and make PCOS symptoms worse.
diagnosisList: Ask about your periods and symptoms
Suggest an ultrasound scan if needed
ArticlePcos.lifestyleIntro: A healthy lifestyle is the most important treatment.
lifestyleList: Eat more vegetables, fruits, whole grains, pulses, and lean protein
Reduce sweets, sugary drinks, and junk food
Exercise for at least 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week
Losing even a small amount of weight can improve periods and increase the chance of pregnancy
ArticlePcos.mantra: My mantra: Eat less, walk more!
medicinesList: Help with acne or unwanted hair growth
Help you become pregnant if you are planning a baby
ArticlePcos.medicinesNote: Always take medicines only as advised by us or the concerned doctor.
ArticlePcos.regularIntro: If PCOS is not treated, it may increase the risk of:
regularList: Cancer of the uterus (womb) if periods are absent for a long time
ArticlePcos.regularClosing: Regular check-ups help prevent these problems.
visitList: Do not get your period for more than 3 months (and are not pregnant)
Have very heavy or prolonged bleeding
Are trying to become pregnant without success
Notice rapid weight gain, severe acne, or increased facial hair
rememberList: Healthy eating, regular exercise, and taking medicines as prescribed can control PCOS
Regular follow-up with your doctor is important to keep you healthy
It will reduce future health problems like diabetes, high blood pressure, and some gynecological cancers

ArticleWhatIvf.metaTitle: What IVF really is — a step-by-step guide
ArticleWhatIvf.metaDescription: A plain-language guide to IVF at IVF Master — the six phases from preparing your body to the pregnancy test, and the support around you at every step.
ArticleWhatIvf.title: What IVF really is
ArticleWhatIvf.intro1: Think of IVF as a way to help nature along. “In vitro” simply means “outside body” or in a laboratory. In short, we take eggs from the ovaries and mix them with sperm or inject the sperm in eggs (ICSI) in our lab to create embryos. We then place the healthiest embryo back into your uterus when it is ready for its acceptance.

phases.heading: Phase 1 — Preparing your body
phases.intro: Before we begin the actual IVF cycle, we need to understand your unique reproductive health. This preparation stage ensures we customise the treatment plan specifically for you.
phases.intro2: Like plants, always good preparation of land before sowing the seeds gives the best yield, this phase is also very crucial.

items.label: Ovarian reserve testing
items.body: It is done by simple blood tests and pelvic ultrasound on day 2 or 3 of menses.

items.label: Semen analysis
items.body: We test a semen sample to check the count, shape, and movement of the sperm. You can see the them on screen.

items.label: Uterine exam
items.body: We examine the inside of your uterus using an ultrasound or a small 4 mm hysteroscope to ensure, the inner lining is safe to welcome an embryo.

items.label: Lifestyle modifications
items.body: We will ask you to start taking prenatal vitamins, maintain a balanced diet, avoid alcohol, and stop smoking.

phases.heading: Phase 2 — Ovarian stimulation (growing the eggs)
phases.intro: In a natural monthly cycle, your body usually matures just one or two eggs. For IVF, we want to grow multiple eggs at once to increase your chances of success.

items.label: Hormone injections
items.body: You can take these yourself, under the skin of your belly or thigh to encourage your ovaries to grow multiple egg follicles.

items.label: Regular monitoring
items.body: You will visit our clinic 2/3 times to monitor the progress. Along with blood tests and ultrasounds we will be able to watch the follicles grow and adjust your medication doses safely.

items.label: The trigger shot
items.body: Once the follicles reach the ideal size, you will take one final, precisely timed injection referred as “trigger shot” which will bring the eggs to full maturity, ready for collection.

phases.note: No need of daily visits to clinic.

phases.heading: Phase 3 — Egg retrieval (the collection)
phases.intro: The egg retrieval is a minor surgical procedure performed at our clinic. It takes about 20 minutes, and you will not feel any pain during the process as it is done under a light anaesthetic or sedative so that you are completely asleep and comfortable.

items.label: Ultrasound guidance
items.body: I will insert a thin ultrasound probe into the vagina to clearly see your ovaries and the mature follicles.

items.label: Gentle suction
items.body: Using a very fine, specialized needle attached to the ultrasound probe, I gently draw the fluid—and the egg inside it—out of each follicle.

items.label: Recovery
items.body: You will rest for an hour or two and will be discharged same day.

phases.heading: Phase 4 — Fertilisation and embryo development
phases.intro: While you are resting from your retrieval, our embryologist takes over the next steps. This is where the magic happens behind the scenes over the next 3 to 6 days.

items.label: IVF with conventional insemination
items.body: We place thousands of healthy sperm in a dish alongside the retrieved eggs and let them fertilise naturally.

items.label: ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection)
items.body: If the sperm count is low or weak, our embryologist will use a tiny needle to inject a single, healthy sperm directly into each mature egg to help it fertilise.

items.label: The incubation phase
items.body: The fertilised eggs become embryos. We place them in advanced incubators that mimic the warmth and environment of a human body, monitoring their growth as they divide into multiple cells.

phases.heading: Phase 5 — The embryo transfer
phases.intro: The embryo transfer is the simplest and most exciting part of the medical process.

items.label: Selecting the best embryo
items.body: Together, we will choose 1 or 2 healthiest embryos to transfer. Remaining high-quality embryos can be frozen for your future use.

items.label: The procedure
items.body: Under abdominal ultrasound guidance, embryo/s will be transferred using a very soft, smallest catheter. You can witness this live on screen.

items.label: Immediate return to routine
items.body: The transfer takes less than 10 minutes. You can get up right away, walk around, and go home to rest. You do not need strict bed rest, but we recommend avoiding heavy lifting or intense workouts and lumpy bumpy journey.

phases.heading: Phase 6 — The 15 days wait
phases.intro: The final phase requires the most patience. Correct and timely usage of progesterone medications along with other supportive medicines help embryo implant into the uterine lining naturally.

items.label: Managing anxiety
items.body: This waiting period can feel emotionally difficult. We encourage you to focus on light activities, stay connected with loved ones. Surrender to Supreme Nature and pamper yourself; this will help you to fulfil your dream of parenthood.

items.label: The official pregnancy test
items.body: In case of day 3 embryo transfer, the hormone HCG is measured in blood to confirm the pregnancy 16 days after the transfer. While, 14 days after in case of day 5 transfer.

ArticleWhatIvf.closingPara1: IVF is a physical journey, but it is also an emotional rollercoaster. Our entire clinical team, including our dedicated nursing staff and counsellors, are here to support you through every single step, question, and milestone.
ArticleWhatIvf.closingPara2: If you are ready to begin, our next step is to schedule your initial consultation and baseline blood tests. Let's take this journey together, one step at a time.

ArticleMyths.metaTitle: IVF myths vs facts — ten common myths, honestly answered
ArticleMyths.metaDescription: Ten of the most common IVF myths, and what is actually true — clear, honest answers from the team at IVF Master.
ArticleMyths.title: 10 IVF myths of IVF
ArticleMyths.intro: Myths about IVF travel fast — and they often cause more worry than they need to. Here are ten of the most common ones, and what is actually true.

items.fact: IVF gives hope, but it does not guarantee pregnancy. Success depends on factors like age, egg quality, sperm quality, and overall health.
Fertility problems can happen in both men and women. IVF can help when the problem is with the woman, the man, or both.
Not anymore. Today, doctors often transfer just one healthy embryo, so most IVF pregnancies result in a single baby.
IVF babies are just as healthy and loved as naturally conceived babies. Millions of healthy IVF babies have been born worldwide.
Most women feel only mild discomfort. The egg collection procedure is done under anesthesia, so you won't feel pain during it.
Feeling worried or emotional is normal. Stress alone does not cause IVF to fail, but taking care of your mental health is important.

items.myth: You need complete bed rest after embryo transfer.
items.fact: No. Normal daily activities are safe. Your doctor may only ask you to avoid heavy exercise or lifting.
Age is one of the most important factors. Younger eggs usually have a better chance of leading to a healthy pregnancy.
Current research shows no strong evidence that IVF treatment causes cancer.

items.myth: A healthy lifestyle doesn't matter during IVF.
items.fact: Eating healthy, getting enough sleep, avoiding smoking/ alcohol will improve results.

ArticleMyths.closing: Talk to us and the supporting team to understand the treatment plan that is best for you.

ArticleMaleFertility.metaDescription: Male-factor infertility is common and often very treatable. The causes, the simple checks, and what men can do to help.
ArticleMaleFertility.title: Male fertility, explained
ArticleMaleFertility.intro: When a couple is finding it hard to conceive, it is not only a question for the woman. Male-factor infertility — when a man has difficulty helping his partner conceive after about a year of trying, with regular unprotected sex — is common, and it deserves the same care and attention. The encouraging news is that it is often very treatable. Here is what can affect male fertility, how we check it, and what you can do to help.

sections.heading: What is male factor Infertility?
sections.body: Male infertility means a man has trouble helping his partner become pregnant, even after trying for 1 year with regular unprotected sex.

sections.heading: What causes it?
items: Low sperm count
Weak or slow-moving sperm
Blockage in the sperm tubes
Infection
Hormone problems
Smoking, alcohol, drugs, or some medicines
Being overweight
Swollen veins around the testicles (Varicocele)

sections.heading: What are the signs?
sections.body: Most men do not have any symptoms. The only sign may be difficulty having a baby.

sections.heading: How is it checked?
items: A physical examination
A semen test (to check sperm)
Blood tests for hormones and general health
An ultrasound if needed

sections.heading: Can it be treated?
sections.intro: Yes. Treatment depends on the cause and may include:
items: Medicines
Surgery (if needed)
Healthy lifestyle changes
Fertility treatments if required

sections.heading: What can you do?
items: Stop smoking and avoid tobacco
Limit or avoid alcohol.
Eat healthy food
Exercise regularly.
Maintain a healthy weight
Get enough sleep.
Avoid too much heat around the testicles.

sections.heading: When should you see a doctor?
items: You have problems with erection or ejaculation
You have been trying for 1 year and no pregnancy
You have pain or swelling in the testicles.

ArticleMaleFertility.closing: Remember: Male infertility is common, and many men can be treated successfully.

ArticleRecurrentLoss.metaTitle: Recurrent pregnancy loss — causes, tests, and treatment
ArticleRecurrentLoss.metaDescription: Recurrent miscarriage is more common than many realise. The causes, the tests, and what can be done — explained with care.
ArticleRecurrentLoss.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss
ArticleRecurrentLoss.intro: Recurrent pregnancy loss means having two or more miscarriages. It is more common than many people realize, and in many cases, a healthy pregnancy is still possible.

sections.heading: Why does it happen?
items: Problems with the baby's chromosomes (most common)
Problems with the shape of the uterus
Hormone problems (such as thyroid disease or diabetes)
Certain blood-clotting or immune conditions
Sometimes, no cause is found

sections.heading: What tests may be needed?
items: Blood tests for associated medical conditions
An ultrasound scan of the uterus
Tests for certain medical conditions
Special tests for APLAS, ANA, ENA or thrombophilia markers.
Sometimes, genetic tests for the couple or the pregnancy tissue

sections.heading: Can it be treated?
sections.intro: Yes. Treatment depends on the cause and may include:
items: Medicines for thyroid disease, diabetes, or blood-clotting disorders
Surgery to correct some uterine problems
Close monitoring during the next pregnancy

sections.heading: What are the chances of a healthy baby?
sections.body: The good news is that most women with recurrent pregnancy loss go on to have a healthy baby, especially with proper medical care and follow-up.

sections.heading: When should you see a doctor?
sections.body: If you have had two or more miscarriages, consult an obstetrician or fertility specialist for evaluation and advice.

ArticleRecurrentLoss.closing: Remember: Having recurrent miscarriages does not mean you cannot have a successful pregnancy. Early medical care and support can improve your chances.

ArticleUnexplained.metaTitle: Unexplained Infertility — Causes, Tests, and Options
ArticleUnexplained.metaDescription: Unexplained infertility is frustrating, but it does not mean pregnancy is impossible. Learn about why it happens and what treatments are available.
ArticleUnexplained.title: Unexplained infertility
ArticleUnexplained.intro: Unexplained infertility means that a couple is having difficulty getting pregnant, even though all the routine fertility tests are normal.

sections.heading: This means:
items: The woman's eggs are being released regularly (ovulation is normal).
The fallopian tubes are open.
The uterus looks healthy.
The man's sperm test is normal.

sections.body: Even though everything appears normal, pregnancy is still not happening. This does not mean that pregnancy is impossible. It simply means that the exact reason cannot be found with the tests we have today.

sections.heading: Can pregnancy still happen?
sections.body: Yes. Many couples with unexplained infertility become pregnant naturally or with fertility treatment.

sections.heading: What are the treatment options?
sections.intro: Depending on your age and how long you have been trying, your doctor may suggest:
items: Trying naturally for a little longer.
Medicines to help improve the chances of pregnancy.
IUI (Intrauterine Insemination), where specially prepared sperm is placed inside the uterus.
IVF (Test Tube Baby) if other treatments are not successful.

ArticleUnexplained.closing: Important message: Having unexplained infertility does not mean you can never have a baby. It only means that the cause has not been identified with current tests. Your fertility specialist will guide you on the best treatment based on your age, medical history, and how long you have been trying to conceive.

ArticleAge.metaTitle: Age and IVF Success Rates — The Facts Explained
ArticleAge.metaDescription: As women get older, IVF success rates decline. Learn how age impacts egg quality, challenges to expect, and what can improve your chances.
ArticleAge.title: Age and IVF success
ArticleAge.intro: As women get older, it becomes harder to become pregnant naturally or through IVF. This is because both the number and quality of eggs decrease with age.

sections.heading: Common Challenges in IVF with Increasing Age
items: Fewer eggs are available during treatment.
Eggs may not fertilize as well.
Fewer healthy embryos are formed.
Lower chance of embryo implantation.
Higher chance of miscarriage.
More than one IVF cycle may be needed.
Pregnancy complications, such as high blood pressure and diabetes, are more common in older mothers.

sections.heading: What Can Help?
items: Do not delay fertility treatment if you are planning a pregnancy.
Maintain a healthy weight, eat a balanced diet, exercise regularly, and avoid smoking and alcohol.
Follow your doctor's advice regarding medications and treatment.
In some cases, genetic testing of embryos or using donor eggs may improve the chance of a healthy pregnancy.

sections.heading: Typical IVF success trends by maternal age (using own eggs)

headers: General live birth chance per IVF cycle*

sections.body: These are approximate ranges and vary by clinic, diagnosis, embryo quality, and individual health.

ArticleAge.closing: Key Message: Age is one of the most important factors affecting IVF success. Starting treatment earlier generally gives a better chance of pregnancy. However, every woman is different, and many women still achieve successful pregnancies with the right treatment and care.
